extracted.intended_audience: TMLR authors, reviewers, and action editors evaluating submissions
extracted.subtask_description: The Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR) acceptance-criteria page lays out the two literal criteria that should govern accept/reject decisions for TMLR submissions, together with explicit elaborations on what reviewers should and should not consider (notably ruling out novelty, significance, or state-of-the-art performance as required criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-criterion acceptance basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of a submission to TMLR should be based on positive answers to the following two questions: (1) Are the claims made in the submission supported by accurate, convincing and clear evidence? (2) Would some individuals in TMLR's audience be interested in the findings of this paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the only two literal acceptance criteria for TMLR; reviewers and action editors are explicitly directed to base their decisions on positive answers to both questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims supported by accurate, convincing and clear evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the claims made in the submission supported by accurate, convincing and clear evidence? This is the most important criterion. This implies assessing the technical soundness as well as the clarity of the narrative and arguments presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is identified as the most important criterion. It covers both technical soundness and clarity of the narrative and arguments used to present the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address gaps between claims and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any gap between claims and evidence should be addressed by the authors. Often, this will lead reviewers to ask the authors to provide more evidence by running more experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are expected to flag gaps between claims and supporting evidence, and the default remedy is to request additional experiments from the authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting (reducing) claims as an alternative to more experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: However, this is not the only way to address such concerns. Another is simply for the authors to adjust (reduce) their claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicitly notes that when evidence is partial, authors may resolve the gap by reducing the scope of their claims rather than running additional experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience interest as subjective criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Would some individuals in TMLR's audience be interested in the findings of this paper? This is arguably the most subjective criterion, and therefore needs to be treated carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are warned that this criterion is subjective and must be applied carefully rather than mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve ambiguity in favor of acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, a reviewer that is unsure as to whether a submission satisfies this criterion should assume that it does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt about audience interest, the default is to assume the criterion is met, biasing toward acceptance rather than rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / impact is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Crucially, it should not be used as a reason to reject work that isn't considered "significant" or "impactful" because it isn't achieving a new state-of-the-art on some benchmark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of state-of-the-art results or perceived impact is explicitly disallowed as a rejection reason under the audience-interest criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty is not a necessary criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor should it form the basis for rejecting work on a method considered not "novel enough", as novelty of the studied method is not a necessary criteria for acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are explicitly told that perceived lack of novelty is not a valid basis for rejection at TMLR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'significant', 'impactful', 'novel'; focus on 'interest'
rubrics_metrics.description: We explicitly avoid these terms ("significant", "impactful", "novel"), and focus instead on the notion of "interest".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMLR explicitly replaces the vocabulary of significance/impact/novelty with the notion of audience interest as the operative concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors making interest evident satisfies the criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If the authors make it clear that there is something to be learned by some researchers in their area from their work, then the criterion of interest is considered satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The threshold for audience interest is satisfied as soon as the paper communicates that some subset of researchers in the area can learn something from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifications handle significance/impact, not acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: TMLR instead relies on certifications (such as "Featured" and "Outstanding") to provide annotations on submissions that pertain to (more speculative) assertions on significance or potential for impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculative judgments about significance and impact are routed to optional certifications, not to the accept/reject decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: class report re-running experiments (insufficient interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine learning class report that re-runs the experiments of a published paper has educational value to the students involved. But if it doesn't surface generalizable insights, it is unlikely to be of interest to (even a subset of) the TMLR audience, and so could be rejected based on this criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example of the interest criterion: pure replication without generalizable insight is grounds for rejection under interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: reproducibility report with actionable lessons (sufficient interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the other hand, a proper reproducibility report that systematically studies the robustness or generalizability of a published method and lays out actionable lessons for its audience could satisfy this criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked counterexample: a reproducibility study that yields generalizable, actionable lessons satisfies the interest criterion.
